transcript: one of the most monumental changes to a Broadway show I've ever seen take place during the preview process was not with a brand new show but with the Tony winning revival of once on this island so monumental in fact that in my opinion it completely reframed the point of the story welcome to another episode of Overthinking Theatre Throwback where I do retrospectives on recent theatre history just as a quick background once on this island is a musical from 1990 based on the book My Love, My Love by Rosa Guy and it's a loose retelling of the Little Mermaid story but about color and class divisions in the Caribbean and as many of you may remember it received a pretty stunning Broadway revival in 2017 directed by Michael Arden it was staged in the round at the circle in the Square Theatre they had real sand on stage real water, live animals the extraordinary cast featured among others Alex Newell and Lea Salonga and the whole show was just a really thrilling experience but when I saw the production in early previews there was one more big theatrical flourish that most people didn't get to see and heads up this does contain spoilers for the plot of the musical if that's something you care about so in the finale of the show they had this large ensemble of children come on stage and play together, dance together and gather around to hear the story of Ti Moune passed down these children were from the program Rosie's Kids which was founded by Rosie O'Donnell and among the children on stage there was seemingly a pretty deliberate mix of white children and children of color which is important to what I'm gonna say cause here's the thing about once on this island it's a beautiful show and in many ways a beautiful story but it does end with the female protagonist sort of sacrificing her life for the man that she loves which looked at through a modern lens is maybe not the most palatable ending and I think what the inclusion of the Rosie's Kids ensemble did was shifted the focus of Ti Moune’s sacrifice because the backdrop of this story is that it is this community divided by skin color and she was a dark skinned woman who fell in love with a light skinned man and I think seeing this ensemble of children gather together across color lines to honor and retell the story of Ti Moune sort of suggested that perhaps what was so beautiful about her sacrifice wasn't that she was just so devoted to her love of this man but that it was a love that sought to break down those barriers it emphasised that as being her lasting legacy now does that completely remove any problematic elements of the show or the ending? I don't know, debatable but I do think it made a big difference in how the ending landed and by extension kind of how the whole story landed unfortunately whether it was for budgeting reasons or logistics they did decide to cut the Rosie's Kids ensemble from the show completely thereby removing that interpretive spin from the ending in many ways it ended up working out for them they were able to run for a little over a year they won the Tony Award for Best Revival and a lot of well deserved acclaim but here and there the question did pop up about like is this a good message to be leaving us with at the end of the show? I don't think this necessarily dominated the conversation around the show but I was acutely aware of it every time it came up because I would say “well, wait till you hear about this thing they did in previews”
